\section{Institutional Background}

\subsubsection*{The Critical Access Hospital Program} The Balanced Budget Act of 1997 created the CAH designation to stem rural hospital closures \citep{BBA1997}.

Hospitals meeting four criteria---location in a rural area, 25 or fewer acute care beds, average length of stay at or below 96 hours, and distance of at least 35 miles from the nearest hospital (or state certification as a ``necessary provider'')---receive 101\% of their reasonable costs from Medicare, rather than the prospective payment rates that govern other hospitals \citep{GAO2018}.

The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 raised the bed limit from 15 to 25, creating a natural experiment that expanded the incentive to a wider range of small hospitals \citep{MMA2003}.
As of 2023, approximately 1,350 hospitals hold CAH designation, representing nearly a quarter of all US hospitals \citep{MedPAC2023}.

\subsubsection*{The 50-Bed RHC and REH Thresholds} The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 established that provider-based Rural Health Clinics (RHCs) at hospitals with fewer than 50 beds are exempt from the per-visit payment cap that constrains freestanding RHCs \citep{BBA2018}.

In addition, the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021 created the Rural Emergency Hospital (REH) designation, allowing hospitals with 50 or fewer beds to convert to emergency-only facilities with enhanced Medicare payments \citep{CAA2021}.

\subsubsection*{The 100-Bed DSH Formula} Under Medicare's Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) adjustment, hospitals with 100 or more beds that serve a disproportionate share of low-income patients use a more generous payment formula than smaller hospitals \citep{MedPAC2019}.

\section{Institutional Background}

Prevailing wage laws --- often called ``Little Davis-Bacon Acts'' after their federal analog enacted in 1931 --- require contractors on publicly funded construction projects to pay workers at least the ``prevailing wage'' in the relevant locality, typically determined by surveys of union wage rates \citep{thieblot1975davisbacon}.

\citet{bernstein1993davisbacon} argued that the federal Davis-Bacon Act was enacted partly to prevent Black workers from undercutting White wages on federal construction, making the law discriminatory in origin.

\section{Institutional Background}

\subsubsection*{The Old Regime} The Anti-Social Behaviour Order was introduced by the Crime and Disorder Act 1998 as Labour's signature response to low-level disorder \citep{burney2002}.

Over the following 15 years, Parliament added 18 additional tools---drinking banning orders, dispersal orders, crack house closure orders, litter clearing notices, designated public place orders, and more---creating what the Home Office itself described as a ``confusing'' and ``bureaucratic'' landscape \citep{homeoffice2014guide}.
By 2013, Greater Manchester had issued 2,197 ASBOs---more than any other area outside London---while Dyfed-Powys issued only 59 \citep{homeoffice2014}.

This variation reflected genuine differences in enforcement philosophy: forces like Greater Manchester and Merseyside built dedicated ASB units, trained specialist prosecutors, and developed court relationships around the ASBO process \citep{solanki2006}.

\subsubsection*{The 2014 Reform} The Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014 received Royal Assent on 13 March 2014 and its main provisions commenced on 20 October 2014 \citep{homeoffice2014guide}.

The reform replaced all 19 existing tools with 6 new powers:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Civil Injunction} (replacing ASBOs on application)
  \item \textbf{Criminal Behaviour Order} (replacing ASBOs on conviction)
  \item \textbf{Community Protection Notice} (replacing litter clearing, defacement removal, street litter control)
  \item \textbf{Public Spaces Protection Order} (replacing designated public place orders, gating orders, dog control orders)
  \item \textbf{Closure Power} (replacing crack house closure, noisy premises closure, s.161 closure)
  \item \textbf{Dispersal Power} (replacing dispersal orders under s.30 ASB Act 2003)
\end{enumerate}

The stated goal was to ``put victims first'' by making powers ``faster, more effective, and easier to use'' \citep{homeoffice2014guide}.
